rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Buhturi’s two-rains couplet does not illustrate joining literal and metaphorical meanings in a dual construction: both praised men are metaphors for rain.
rows.anchor: غيثان إن جدب تتابع أقبلا وهما ربيع مؤمل وخريفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding Al-Buhturi’s couplet about two lions makes the example fit: one lion is real and the other is metaphorical.
rows.anchor: فلم أر ضرغامين أصدق منكما عراكا إذا الهيابة النكس كذبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although generic rain leaves no literal individual to pair with al-Farazdaq’s father, the comparison abstracts rain’s shared benefit; treating the genus as one entity makes the pairing like calling people suns.
rows.anchor: ولكن على أصل في التشبيه وهو أن يقصد إلى المعنى الذي من أجله يشبه الفرع بالأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sentence conveys information through affirmation or negation; a single noun or verb cannot supply that predicative relation by itself.
rows.anchor: مدار الفائدة في الحقيقة على الإثبات والنفي ألا ترى أن الخبر أول معاني الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affirmation and negation each require two terms: what is predicated and what it is predicated of, corresponding to subject and predicate or verb and agent; these are musnad and musnad ilayh.
rows.anchor: كان ذانك الشيئان المبتدأ والخبر والفعل والفاعل وقيل للمثبت وللمنفى مسند وحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even “Zayd struck” needs two restrictions—affirming striking, then affirming it of Zayd; neither an unqualified judgment nor a judgment restricted only to one thing yields a complete proposition.
rows.anchor: قولك إثبات الضرب تقييد للإثبات بإضافته إلى الضرب ثم لا يكفيك هذا التقييد حتى تقيده مرة أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True wealth is freedom from need; a rich person whose greed keeps generating new wants remains needy, like the glutton who eats but is never satisfied.
rows.anchor: حقيقة الغنى هو انتفاء الحاجة والحاجة أن تريد الشيء ولا تجده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A miser may be unable to use the wealth he owns; real wealth requires generosity, sound judgment, and resolve to control and spend one’s possessions, as al-Buhturi’s verse illustrates.
rows.anchor: لأنه عدم كرما يبسط أنامله وجودا ينصر آمله وعقلا ينصره وهمة تمكنه مما لديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Custom calls abundant money wealth and little money poverty because money tends to satisfy wants, but this names the cause for its effect; the true meanings are absence and presence of need.
rows.anchor: فهو من جنس تسمية السبب باسم المسبب وإلا فحقيقة الغنى انتفاء الاحتياج وحقيقة الفقر الاحتياج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone is truly rich, since need is impossible for Him and He is exalted above the attributes of created beings.
rows.anchor: والله تعالى الغنى على الحقيقة لاستحالة الاحتياج عليه جل وتعالى عن صفات المخلوقين

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet distinguishes worldly insolvency from the true bankrupt person: one arrives with worship but has wronged others, whose claims consume his good deeds before their sins are placed on him.
rows.anchor: رسول الله قال أتدرون ما المفلس قالوا المفلس فينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the afterlife good deeds function like worldly wealth because they bring felicity and avert punishment; someone stripped of them is therefore truly bankrupt.
rows.anchor: لما كان الإنسان إنما يعد غنيا في الدنيا بماله لأنه يجتلب به المسرة ويدفع المضرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some comparisons are wholly imaginary: ruby standards with emerald shafts and pearl vessels containing carnelian are not objects one encounters in reality, especially when the ruby is imagined unfurled.
rows.anchor: فليس في العادة أن تتخذ صورة أعلاها ياقوت على مقدار العلم وتحت ذلك الياقوت قطع مطاولة من الزبرجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the image of dawn throwing off its garment, the garment is moved aside to expose most of the body, not removed entirely; otherwise the comparison would concern dawn alone and clash with dawn appearing beneath night.
rows.anchor: في إلقاء الجل أن تريد أنه أداره عن ظهره وأزاله عن مكانه حتى تكشف أكثر جسده لا أنه رمى به جملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lightning and piebald image concerns a sudden flash, like white patches appearing when a horse leaps and its covering shifts, rather than a simple comparison of lightning’s color; Ibn Babak offers a parallel.
rows.anchor: ينبغي أن يكون الغرض بذكر الجل أن البرق يلمع بغتة ويلوح للعين فجأة فصار لذلك كبياض الأبلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Muʿtazz’s “when it leapt” adds force, while an earlier poet’s prancing and circling horses preserve the chief basis of resemblance: their movement and the manner of the flash.
rows.anchor: وقد عنى المتقدمون أيضا بمثل هذا الاحتياط ألا تراه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second kind of comparison depicts things that can exist, though some are common and others rare; the stars scattered like pearls on a blue carpet illustrate this kind.
rows.anchor: هذا القسم الثاني الذي يدخل في الوجود يتفاوت حاله فمنه ما يتسع وجوده ومنه ما يوجد في النادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wordplay and rhymed prose succeed when the meaning leads the speaker to them; removing them would then make the expression awkward, unlike an effect imposed on the meaning.
rows.anchor: أن المتكلم لم يقد المعنى نحو التجنيس والسجع بل قادة المعنى إليهما وعبر به الفرق عليهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soundest practice is to let meanings follow their own course and find fitting words; deciding in advance to pun or rhyme with chosen words risks affectation and error.
rows.anchor: أن ترسل المعاني على سجيتها وتدعها تطلب لانفسها الالفاظ فانها إذا تركت وما تريد لم تكنس إلا ما يليق بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The naturally arising wordplay in the cited “أودعاني” line and Abu Tammam’s Najd and “الحمام” couplets shows how a meaning can happen to invite a pun.
rows.anchor: كما ساعد أبا تمام في نحو قوله ( وأنجدتم من بعد إتهام داركم فيا دمع أنجدني على ساكني نجد )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Tammam treats every place-name as an obligation to devise a pun, producing contrived examples; such forced wordplay, like the later poet’s “داء” conceit, invites criticism.
rows.anchor: أسلم نفسه للتكلف ويرى انه إن مر على اسم موضع يحتاج إلى ذكره أو يتصل بقصة يذكرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem’s categorical claim that the beloved is the sun makes her celestial abode proof that reaching her is impossible, presenting the fact itself rather than an explicit simile.
rows.anchor: ألا تراه كأنه يقول للنفس ما وجه الطمع في الوصول وقد علمت أن حديثك مع الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abi ʿUyaynah’s poem does not deny the comparison: it says she is the sun, then contrasts the nearness of its light with the difficulty of reaching it.
rows.anchor: بيت ابن أبي عيينه في أن لم ينصرف عن التشبيه جملة ولم يبرز في صورة الجاحد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bashshar and al-Mutanabbi state their comparisons openly, respectively likening the beloved to a distant moon and to the sun whose rays approach but cannot be grasped.
rows.anchor: كبيت بشار الذي صرح فيه بالتشبيه وهو ( أو كبدر السماء غير قريب حين يوفى والضوء فيه اقتراب )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although mentioning the sun conventionally suggests beauty, in these examples the direct aim is to explain nearness in one respect and distance in another; beauty is only a customary secondary implication.
rows.anchor: يقصد فيها إلى بيان أمر غير الحسن يصير كالشىء الذي يعقل من طريق العرف وعلى سبيل التبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling a praised person “night” is not idiomatic merely to express displeasure; the metaphor suits someone described through darkness or blackness, as in Ibn Tabataba’s verse about a dark-skinned man.
rows.anchor: العرف لم يجر بأن تجعل الممدوح ليلا هكذا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet gives explicit comparisons: people are like a hundred camels with no mount among them, and the believer is like a palm or a young shoot.
rows.anchor: قول النبي الناس كإبل مائة لا تجد فيها فيها راحلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An explicit simile cannot always become a metaphor by deleting the subject: reading the Prophet’s camels as people or a palm as a believer would be a strained riddle, not ordinary speech.
rows.anchor: هل تقدر أن تقول رأيت إبلا مائة لا تجد فيها راحلة في معنى رأيت ناسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With an explicit kāf-simile the comparison noun is normally definite, while an indefinite needs a qualifying adjective; as a predicate, however, both definite and indefinite forms are natural.
rows.anchor: كان كلا الأمرين التعريف والتنكير فيه حسنا جميلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the eye is indispensable to a lookout’s task, its name can stand for the whole person, as though the eye were the person himself.
rows.anchor: العين لما كانت المقصودة في كون الرجل ربيئة صارت كأنها الشخص كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names can transfer through causal relations: rain is treated as the vegetation it produces, while rain is called “sky” because it descends from the sky; such links vary in strength and clarity.
rows.anchor: والغيث لما كان النبت يكون عنه صار كانه هو والمطر لما كان ينزل من السماء عبروا عنه باسمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the slaughtered sheep an ʿaqīqah has a stronger relation than calling a cry an ʿaqīrah, which arose accidentally; the latter resembles a proverb repeated after the fact, such as “summer, you squandered the milk.”
rows.anchor: الشاة التي تذبح عن الصبي إذا حلقت عقيقته عقيقة وتجد حالها بعد أقوى من حال العقيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metaphor is broader than istiʿārah: every istiʿārah is a metaphor, but not every metaphor is an istiʿārah.
rows.anchor: أن أبين أن المجاز أعم من الاستعارة وان الصحيح من القضية في ذلك أن كل استعارة مجاز وليس كل مجاز استعارة

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Qadi Abu al-Hasan defines istiʿārah through closeness and affinity of resemblance; al-Jurjani cites this conventional definition to explain its narrower transfer of a name through simile and hyperbole.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو الحسن في أثناء فصل ذكرها فيه وملاك الاستعارة تقريب الشبه ومناسبة المستعار للمستعار منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reordering the opening of Imruʾ al-Qays’s poem turns eloquent verse into nonsense and severs its attribution, showing that its identity depends on a particular arrangement of words.
rows.anchor: منزل قفا ذكرى من نبك حبيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meaningful composition of words follows meanings arranged in the mind according to reason; sentence roles impose ordering, such as an interrogative’s precedence and an adjective’s following its noun.
rows.anchor: المعنى الذي له كانت هذه الكلم بيت شعر أو فصل خطاب هو ترتيبها على طريقة معلومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When critics praise wording as sweet or elegant, they are not judging its sounds or basic lexical form but an effect in the heart and a distinction produced by the intellect.
rows.anchor: ليس ينبئك عن أحوال ترجع إلى أجراس الحروف وإلى ظاهر الوضع اللغوي بل إلى أمر يقع من المرء في فؤاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Word choice can also be praised independently of meaning when it is familiar in current usage rather than strange or vulgar; sometimes the fault called vulgarity belongs to the meaning instead.
rows.anchor: اللفظة مما يتعارفه الناس في استعمالهم ويتداولونه في زمانهم ولا يكون وحشيا غريبا أو عاميا سخيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet treats the moon’s effect on linen as a known fact: he explains the garment’s rapid wear by saying its buttons have been fastened onto the moon.
rows.anchor: قد عمد كما ترى إلى شيء هو خاصية في طبيعة القمر وأمر غريب من تأثيره ثم جعل يرى أن قوما انكروا بلى الكتان بسرعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The simile is so suppressed that the poem argues from the moon as though it were literally involved; making the comparison explicit would weaken the image and destroy its proof against wonder.
rows.anchor: وأن التشبيه قد نسى وانسى وصار كما يقول الشيخ أبو على فيما يتعلق به الطرف إنه شريعة منسوخة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another poet attributes linen’s wear to constant moonlight, but his wording does not claim the moon’s causal role as forcefully as the first poem.
rows.anchor: إلا أن لفظة لا ينبىء عن القوة التي لهذا البيت في دعوى القمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf likewise makes the metaphorical claim that the beloved is the sun seem factual, then consoles the heart because her dwelling is in the sky.
rows.anchor: قول العباس بن الأحنف ( هي الشمس مسكنها في السماء فعز الفؤاد عزاء جميلا )

rows.speaker: المتنبي
rows.claim: Al-Mutanabbi replaces the ordinary reason for a patron’s killing enemies—removing danger—with the claim that he avoids disappointing the wolves’ hopes.
rows.anchor: مثاله قول المتنبي ( ما به قتل أعاديه ولكن يتقى إخلاف ما ترجو الذئاب )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This invented cause praises extraordinary generosity: the patron goes to war because wolves expect sustenance from the slain and he cannot bear to disappoint those who hope.
rows.anchor: أن يبالغ في وصفه بالسخاء والجود وأن طبيعة الكرم قد غلبت عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author adds that decisive victory prevents enemies from returning and spares further bloodshed; the image also distinguishes the patron from one who kills excessively from rage, while retaining the stated praise of his traits.
rows.anchor: يهزم العدا ويكسرهم كسرا لا يطمعون بعده في المعاودة فيستغنى بذلك عن قتلهم وإراقة دمائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Talib al-Maʾmuni pictures a generous minister sleeping in hope of dreaming a late visitor seeking aid; the author warns that overexplaining the image could imply few people seek his gifts and weaken the praise.
rows.anchor: قول أبى طالب المامونى في قصيدة يمدح بها بعض الوزراء ببخارى
